prompt: What does it mean that right-of-way is "given, not taken"?
choices: The driver who has the right-of-way may keep going even if a crash could result
Right-of-way belongs to whichever vehicle is moving faster
The law says who must yield, but no one may force their way through if a crash could result
Right-of-way rules only apply when a police officer is present
explanation: Right-of-way laws only say who must yield. Even when another driver should yield to you, you must never insist on going first if doing so could cause a crash.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 52, TX p. 26, NV p. 34)

prompt: Do traffic laws give any driver an absolute right to go first?
choices: No. They only say who must yield, and every driver must still try to avoid a crash
Yes. The driver on the main road always has an absolute right to go first
Yes. A green light gives an absolute right to go no matter what
Yes. Once you have stopped at a STOP sign, you always have the right to go next
explanation: Handbooks stress that the law does not give anyone the right-of-way; it only states who must yield. Every driver is still responsible for avoiding a collision.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 52, TX p. 26, NV p. 34)

prompt: You are going straight through an intersection where you have the right-of-way. A driver on a side street pulls out in front of you without yielding. What should you do?
choices: Keep your speed and honk, because you have the right-of-way
Slow down or stop to avoid a crash, even though the other driver was wrong
Speed up to get through before the other car blocks you
Hold your lane and speed so the other driver learns the rule
explanation: Having the right-of-way does not protect you from a crash. If another driver fails to yield, you must still slow or stop to avoid hitting them.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 52, TX p. 26, NV p. 34)

prompt: Another driver is supposed to yield to you at an intersection. What should you do before you go?
choices: Go right away, because the law is on your side
Flash your headlights to tell the driver to stay put, then go without looking
Make sure the other driver is actually stopping or yielding to you
Wait for the other driver to wave before you ever proceed
explanation: Never assume other drivers will give you the right-of-way. Even when you legally have it, confirm the other driver is yielding before you proceed.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 52, TX p. 26, NV p. 34)

prompt: At a four-way stop, another driver arrived first but waves you through. What is the best response?
choices: Go immediately, because the wave means the intersection is clear
You may go if it is safe, but check for other vehicles and pedestrians yourself first
Never accept the wave, because giving up your turn is illegal
Honk to confirm, then go without checking again
explanation: Drivers may give up their right-of-way, and accepting it is allowed. But a wave only means that one driver is waiting; it does not mean the intersection is clear of other traffic or pedestrians.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 52, TX p. 26, NV p. 34)

prompt: Why is failing to yield the right-of-way so dangerous?
choices: It is only a paperwork violation and rarely causes crashes
It only matters on highways, not at intersections
It puts two road users in the same space at the same time, which is a common cause of crashes
It only matters when pedestrians are present
explanation: Right-of-way rules decide who goes first when paths cross. Ignoring them is one of the most common causes of intersection crashes, so handbooks urge drivers to yield whenever in doubt.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 52, TX p. 26, NV p. 34)

prompt: Two vehicles reach an intersection with no signs or signals at about the same time, on different roads. Who must yield?
choices: The driver on the right yields to the driver on the left
The larger vehicle goes first
The driver on the left yields to the driver on the right
The vehicle that is going faster goes first
explanation: At an uncontrolled intersection, when two vehicles arrive at about the same time from different roads, the driver on the left must yield to the driver on the right.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 45, NY p. 34, CO p. 14)

prompt: At an intersection with no signs or signals, a car is already in the intersection when you arrive. Who goes first?
choices: You, if the other car came from your left
Whichever driver is going straight
You, if your street is wider
The car that is already in the intersection
explanation: A vehicle already in the intersection has the right-of-way over vehicles just arriving. Let it clear before you enter.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 45, NY p. 34, CO p. 14)

prompt: What should you do as you approach an intersection that has no signs or signals?
choices: Keep your speed, since no one has to yield at an uncontrolled intersection
Slow down and be ready to stop for traffic coming from either side
Speed up so you spend less time in the intersection
Watch only to your right, since only that traffic matters
explanation: Uncontrolled intersections have no signs telling anyone to stop, so approach slowly, look left and right, and be ready to stop or yield.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 45, NY p. 34, CO p. 14)

prompt: You and a car on your left reach an uncontrolled intersection at about the same time. What should you expect?
choices: You must yield to the car on your left
That driver should yield to you, but be ready to stop in case they do not
You may go at full speed because you have the right-of-way
Whichever driver honks first gets to go first
explanation: The driver on the left yields to the driver on the right, so the other car should let you go. Still, never assume it will; be prepared to stop.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 45, NY p. 34, CO p. 14)

prompt: You reach an uncontrolled intersection at the same time as a car on your right. What should you do?
choices: Go first, since you are on the left
Go first if you are driving straight and the other car is not
Go at the same time, since you both arrived together
Let the car on your right go first
explanation: When two vehicles arrive at about the same time at an intersection without signs or signals, the driver on the left (you) yields to the driver on the right.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 45, NY p. 34, CO p. 14)

prompt: At an uncontrolled intersection, a car is approaching from your right but is still far away. Which statement is correct?
choices: The yield-to-the-right rule is for vehicles arriving at about the same time, so a distant car does not automatically get to go first
You must always wait for every vehicle on your right to pass, however far away it is
Vehicles on your right never matter at an uncontrolled intersection
Right-of-way goes to whichever vehicle is traveling faster
explanation: The driver on the left yields when vehicles arrive at about the same time. If the vehicle on your right is far enough away that you can cross safely, its driver is not entitled to go first, but you must still watch it carefully.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 45, NY p. 34, CO p. 14)

prompt: At a four-way stop, which vehicle should go first?
choices: The vehicle that came to a stop first
The vehicle on the busier road
The vehicle that is going straight
The largest vehicle
explanation: At an all-way stop, every vehicle must stop, and vehicles go in the order they arrived. The first to stop is the first to go.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 52, NJ p. 69, NM p. 14)

prompt: Two cars stop at a four-way stop at the same time, on roads at right angles to each other. Who goes first?
choices: The car on the left
The car on the right
The car that is turning
The car that stopped more smoothly
explanation: When vehicles at right angles arrive at an all-way stop at the same time, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 52, NJ p. 69, NM p. 14)

prompt: You pull up to a four-way stop just after a car on your left has already stopped. What should you do?
choices: Go first, because you are on the other car's right
Stop completely, then let the car on your left go first because it arrived first
Roll through slowly, since the other car is already stopped
Go at the same time as the other car
explanation: Arrival order comes first at an all-way stop. The yield-to-the-right rule only breaks a tie when vehicles arrive at the same time.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 52, NJ p. 69, NM p. 14)

prompt: At a four-way stop, you and the car facing you arrive at the same time. Both of you are going straight. What should happen?
choices: Only one car may move, so the faster driver goes first
You must wait until the other driver waves you through
You must yield, because the other car is on your left
You may each go ahead with caution, since your paths do not cross
explanation: Vehicles facing each other that are both going straight do not cross paths, so both may proceed carefully, watching for any turns.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 52, NJ p. 69, NM p. 14)

prompt: At a four-way stop, you and the car facing you arrive at the same time. You want to turn left, and the other driver is going straight. Who goes first?
choices: You, because you signaled your turn
You, because a left turn clears the intersection faster
Whoever starts moving first
The other driver; you yield before turning left
explanation: A driver turning left must yield to oncoming traffic going straight or turning right. That rule still applies when both vehicles arrive at an all-way stop together.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 52, NJ p. 69, NM p. 14)

prompt: You reach a four-way stop before anyone else. What must you still do before going?
choices: Nothing; arriving first means you may roll through
Come to a complete stop and check for pedestrians and other traffic
Wait until every other approaching car has also stopped
Honk to claim your turn
explanation: Arriving first lets you go first, but only after a full stop, and only after checking that the crosswalks and intersection are clear.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 52, NJ p. 69, NM p. 14)

prompt: You stopped first at a four-way stop. As you start to go, a car on your right rolls through without stopping. What should you do?
choices: Keep going, because you have the right-of-way
Speed up to get across ahead of it
Stop and let it go; avoid the crash even though it was your turn
Keep going and honk so the other driver stops
explanation: The other driver broke the rule, but right-of-way is given, not taken. You must do everything you can to avoid a collision.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 52, NJ p. 69, NM p. 14)

prompt: Three cars stop at an all-way stop at the same time: you, a car on your left, and a car on your right. No one is across from you. Who should go first?
choices: You, because you are in the middle
The car on your left
The car on your right
Whichever car is going straight
explanation: Each driver yields to the vehicle on their right. The car on your left yields to you, you yield to the car on your right, and nobody is to that car's right, so it goes first.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 52, NJ p. 69, NM p. 14)

prompt: You are stopped at a STOP sign, and the cross traffic does not have to stop. When may you go?
choices: As soon as you have come to a full stop
When a driver on the cross street flashes their headlights
After yielding to cross traffic and pedestrians, when there is a safe gap
As soon as the car ahead of you has gone
explanation: Stopping does not give you the right-of-way. After a full stop, you must yield to pedestrians and to cross traffic that is close enough to be a hazard.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 69, NY p. 34, AL p. 65)

prompt: You are stopped at a STOP sign. A car on the cross street, which has no STOP sign, is coming from your left. Who has the right-of-way?
choices: You, because you are on that car's right
The car on the cross street, because you face a STOP sign
You, because you stopped first
Whoever is going straight
explanation: The yield-to-the-right rule only applies when no signs control the intersection or when all approaches must stop. A driver at a STOP sign must yield to cross traffic that does not have to stop.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 69, NY p. 34, AL p. 65)

prompt: You are driving onto a cross street where your road has a YIELD sign. Who has the right-of-way?
choices: Traffic and pedestrians on the cross street; you slow down and stop if needed
You do, as long as you do not stop
You do, if you are turning right
Whoever is driving the larger vehicle
explanation: A YIELD sign means you must slow down and give the right-of-way to vehicles and pedestrians on the road you are entering, stopping if necessary.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 69, NY p. 34, AL p. 65)

prompt: You are on a road that ends at a T-intersection with a STOP sign. A car on the through road is coming from your left. What should you do?
choices: Stay stopped and let it pass before you pull out
Go first, because you are on that car's right
Go first, because the other car should slow down for you
Pull out partway so the other car knows you are there
explanation: A driver at a STOP sign must yield to traffic on the through road, no matter which side it comes from.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 45, AZ p. 35, TX p. 26)

prompt: You reach the end of a road at a T-intersection with no signs. A car on the through road is approaching from your right and will get there at about the same time. Who should go first?
choices: You, because turning vehicles go first
You, because the through-road driver can slow down more easily
Whichever car is smaller
The car on the through road
explanation: The car is on the through road and on your right, so you yield. Handbooks that cover T-intersections give through-road traffic the right-of-way, and the yield-to-the-right rule points the same way.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 45, AZ p. 35, TX p. 26)

prompt: You are turning left at an intersection on a green light, and an oncoming car is going straight. Who has the right-of-way?
choices: You, because you signaled
You, because turning vehicles have priority
Whoever is driving the larger vehicle
The oncoming car going straight
explanation: A driver turning left must yield to oncoming vehicles going straight that are close enough to be a hazard.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 34, NH p. 20, TX p. 26)

prompt: You are waiting to turn left on a solid green light with no arrow. Oncoming cars are close. What should you do?
choices: Wait until oncoming traffic clears or is far enough away to turn safely
Turn now; the green light gives you the right-of-way
Turn quickly before the oncoming cars reach you
Signal and expect oncoming drivers to stop for you
explanation: A green light lets you turn, but you must still yield to oncoming traffic that is close enough to be a hazard.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 34, NH p. 20, TX p. 26)

prompt: You want to turn left into a driveway in the middle of a block. A car is coming toward you. What must you do?
choices: Turn first; oncoming traffic must stop for drivers turning into driveways
Turn when ready, since yield rules apply only at intersections
Stop in your lane and wait for the oncoming driver to wave you on
Yield to the oncoming car if it is close enough to be a hazard
explanation: The left-turn rule also applies to turns into driveways, alleys, parking lots and private roads: yield to oncoming traffic close enough to be a hazard.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 34, NH p. 20, TX p. 26)

prompt: You are turning left at an intersection. An oncoming driver is turning right onto the same street you are turning onto. Who should yield?
choices: The other driver, because right turns always yield to left turns
Whoever starts the turn first
You should, because a left turn yields to oncoming traffic going straight or turning right
The other driver, because you are already in the intersection
explanation: Drivers turning left must yield to oncoming traffic, including vehicles turning right. Let the right-turning car complete its turn first.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 34, NH p. 20, TX p. 26)

prompt: You are turning left on a green arrow. What must you still yield to?
choices: Vehicles and pedestrians that are still in the intersection
Nothing; a green arrow means every other driver must stop
Only vehicles that are larger than yours
Only traffic coming from behind you
explanation: A green arrow protects your turn, but you must still yield to vehicles and pedestrians lawfully in the intersection, such as someone finishing a crossing.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 34, CO p. 14, FL p. 60)

prompt: You are turning left on a green light. A pedestrian is crossing the street you are turning onto. What should you do?
choices: Wait for the pedestrian to finish crossing your path before you turn
Turn in front of the pedestrian, since you have a green light
Honk so the pedestrian hurries
Speed up to get through the crosswalk before they reach your lane
explanation: Turning drivers must yield to pedestrians in the crosswalk they are turning across, even on a green light.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 47, NY p. 34, AZ p. 36)

prompt: You are waiting to turn left on a green light. The oncoming traffic is a single motorcycle that seems far away. What should you keep in mind?
choices: Small vehicles are easy to misjudge, so take time to judge its speed and yield if it is close enough to be a hazard
Motorcycles must yield to turning cars
You can always turn in front of a motorcycle because it can stop quickly
The left-turn rule only applies to cars and trucks
explanation: Left-turning drivers must yield to all oncoming traffic, including motorcycles and bicycles, whose speed and distance are harder to judge.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 34, NH p. 20, TX p. 26)

prompt: Your light turns green, but a car is still in the intersection finishing its turn. What should you do?
choices: Go right away, since your light is green
Honk and go, since it should have waited
Go around the car to keep traffic moving
Let it clear the intersection before you go
explanation: A green light does not cancel the right-of-way of vehicles already in the intersection. Let them clear before you enter.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 34, CO p. 14, FL p. 60)

prompt: Your light turns green while a pedestrian is still crossing in front of you. What should you do?
choices: Go, because the light changed in your favor
Creep forward to signal the pedestrian to hurry
Wait until the pedestrian finishes crossing
Go around the pedestrian if there is room
explanation: If a pedestrian entered the crosswalk before your light changed, you must still yield and let them finish crossing.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 34, CO p. 14, FL p. 60)

prompt: Which statement about a green light is correct?
choices: It gives you the right-of-way over everyone else
It allows you to go, but you must still yield to vehicles and pedestrians already in the intersection
It means pedestrians must wait until you have passed
It means you never need to look before entering
explanation: Signals assign who may go, but drivers on green must still yield to anyone lawfully in the intersection and must avoid crashes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 34, CO p. 14, FL p. 60)

prompt: You are pulling out of a driveway onto a street. Who has the right-of-way?
choices: You do, once your turn signal is on
Traffic on the street and pedestrians on the sidewalk
You do, if the street has only one lane each way
Only the traffic coming from your left
explanation: Drivers entering a road from a driveway, alley, private road or parking lot must yield to all traffic on the road and to pedestrians.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 34, FL p. 70, MT p. 50)

prompt: You are leaving a parking lot and want to turn left onto a two-way street. Whom must you yield to?
choices: Only vehicles coming from your left
Only vehicles coming from your right
No one, if you have signaled your turn
Vehicles coming from both directions, and any pedestrians
explanation: When you enter a street from a parking lot or driveway, you yield to all traffic on the street. A left turn crosses both directions, so you yield to both.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 34, FL p. 70, MT p. 50)

prompt: You are driving out of an alley. A person is walking along the sidewalk across the alley exit. What should you do?
choices: Drive across, because pedestrians must yield to vehicles at alleys
Honk so the pedestrian moves aside
Cross slowly in front of them, since they can see you
Wait for the pedestrian to pass before you cross the sidewalk
explanation: Drivers crossing a sidewalk to enter or leave an alley, driveway or parking lot must yield to pedestrians on the sidewalk.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 34, FL p. 70, MT p. 50)

prompt: You are driving on a main road. A car is waiting to pull out of a driveway on your right. Who has the right-of-way?
choices: You do, but watch in case the driver pulls out anyway
The car in the driveway, because it is on your right
The car in the driveway, because it was there first
Whichever driver honks first
explanation: Vehicles entering from a driveway must yield to traffic on the road. The yield-to-the-right rule does not apply here, but stay alert, because the driver may not see you.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 34, FL p. 70, MT p. 50)

prompt: You are parked at the curb and want to pull back into traffic. Who has the right-of-way?
choices: You do, once you turn on your signal
You do, because drivers behind you must let you in
Whoever is going slower
Traffic already on the road; wait for a safe gap
explanation: When pulling away from a curb, you are entering traffic, so you must yield to vehicles already on the road and move out only when it is safe.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 14, NJ p. 70, AZ p. 31)

prompt: You are backing out of a parking space. Who has the right-of-way?
choices: Vehicles and pedestrians passing behind you
You do, because you started moving first
You do, if your backup camera shows nothing
Only pedestrians, not other vehicles
explanation: A driver who is backing must yield to all vehicles and pedestrians close enough to be a hazard. Check behind you and back slowly.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 34, FL p. 70, MT p. 50)

prompt: Drivers must yield to pedestrians in which crosswalks?
choices: Only crosswalks with painted lines
Only crosswalks with a WALK signal
Only crosswalks near schools
Marked and unmarked crosswalks
explanation: Pedestrians have the right-of-way in both marked and unmarked crosswalks. Not every crosswalk has painted lines.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 47, NY p. 34, AZ p. 36)

prompt: What is an unmarked crosswalk?
choices: Any place in the middle of a block where someone decides to cross
The crossing area at an intersection, between the corners, even when no lines are painted
A crosswalk whose paint has worn off, which drivers may ignore
A crossing that only bicycles may use
explanation: Crosswalks exist at intersections whether or not they are marked with lines. Drivers must yield to pedestrians in them just as in marked crosswalks.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 47, NY p. 34, AZ p. 36)

prompt: You are approaching a corner with no painted crosswalk lines. A pedestrian is crossing the street there. What should you do?
choices: Keep going, because there is no marked crosswalk
Honk to warn the pedestrian to get out of the street
Yield only if the pedestrian has a WALK signal
Yield to the pedestrian, since the corner has an unmarked crosswalk
explanation: An intersection has crosswalks even without painted lines. Drivers must yield to pedestrians crossing at marked or unmarked crosswalks.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 47, NY p. 34, AZ p. 36)

prompt: A car in the lane next to you has stopped at a crosswalk. What should you do?
choices: Pass it carefully, since your lane is clear
Change lanes to go around it
Slow down and stop; do not pass it, because a pedestrian may be crossing
Honk to find out why it stopped
explanation: Never pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk. It may be stopped for a pedestrian you cannot see.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 47, NY p. 34, AZ p. 36)

prompt: A pedestrian is crossing in the middle of the block, not in a crosswalk. What is your duty as a driver?
choices: Keep going; pedestrians outside crosswalks have no protection
Slow down or stop to avoid hitting them, even though they should have yielded
Honk and keep your speed so they move out of the way
Speed up to pass before they reach your lane
explanation: Pedestrians crossing outside a crosswalk are supposed to yield to vehicles, but drivers must still do everything they can to avoid striking them.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 47, NY p. 34, AZ p. 36)

prompt: You are turning right at a green light. A pedestrian is crossing the street you are turning onto. What should you do?
choices: Wait for the pedestrian to cross before you complete the turn
Turn, since you have a green light
Turn behind the pedestrian while they are still in your lane
Honk so the pedestrian knows you are turning
explanation: Drivers turning at an intersection must yield to pedestrians crossing in the crosswalk, even when the driver has a green light.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 47, NY p. 34, AZ p. 36)

prompt: You stop for a pedestrian waiting at a crosswalk on a road with two lanes in your direction. Should you wave the pedestrian across?
choices: Yes. Waving is required to show you are yielding
No. A driver in the other lane may not have stopped, and your wave could lead them into danger
Yes. Once you stop, all other lanes must also be clear
No. Pedestrians must wait until all traffic has passed
explanation: Do not wave pedestrians into traffic. Another driver may not see them or may not stop. Simply stop and let the pedestrian decide when it is safe.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 47, NY p. 34, AZ p. 36)

prompt: When you stop for a pedestrian at a crosswalk, where should your vehicle be?
choices: Partly in the crosswalk, so the pedestrian can see you
Behind the crosswalk, at the stop line if there is one
In the middle of the crosswalk, so other drivers stop too
Past the crosswalk, out of the pedestrian's way
explanation: Stop before the crosswalk (at the stop or limit line if one is marked) so the pedestrian has the full crosswalk to use.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 47, NY p. 34, AZ p. 36)

prompt: Who should you watch for and yield to when you drive through an intersection or turn at a corner?
choices: Only other drivers
Only pedestrians who make eye contact
Only pedestrians at marked school crossings
Pedestrians crossing in the crosswalks
explanation: Drivers must yield to pedestrians legally using marked or unmarked crosswalks, so always check the crosswalks before entering or turning.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 47, NY p. 34, AZ p. 36)

prompt: A pedestrian using a white cane or a guide dog is crossing the street ahead. What must you do?
choices: Honk so they know where you are
Drive around them slowly
Yield, stopping if needed, and let them cross
Yield only if they are in a marked crosswalk
explanation: Pedestrians who are blind or visually impaired, shown by a white cane or guide dog, have the right-of-way. Stop if necessary and let them finish crossing.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 48, NY p. 67, MT p. 49)

prompt: A pedestrian with a white cane starts across even though the signal is against them. What should you do?
choices: Yield and let the pedestrian cross anyway
Proceed, because the signal is in your favor
Honk to warn them to step back
Drive around them if there is room
explanation: A blind pedestrian with a white cane or guide dog must be given the right-of-way even when signals or other right-of-way rules are not in their favor.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 48, NY p. 67, MT p. 49)

prompt: Why should you avoid honking at a pedestrian who is blind?
choices: Honking is the only safe way to warn them
Blind pedestrians cannot hear horns
Honking is only a problem near schools
The noise can confuse or frighten them
explanation: Blind pedestrians rely on sound to judge traffic. A horn can startle or confuse them, so do not honk; simply stop and wait.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 48, NY p. 67, MT p. 49)

prompt: Why is it risky to stop in the middle of a crosswalk when a blind pedestrian is waiting to cross?
choices: It is not risky, because blind pedestrians only cross with a guide
It only matters if the pedestrian has a guide dog
Your engine noise will make them wait longer
They may have to walk around your car, outside the crosswalk and into traffic
explanation: Blocking the crosswalk can force a blind pedestrian to leave it and walk into moving traffic. Stop behind the crosswalk.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 48, NY p. 67, MT p. 49)

prompt: You are driving a quiet hybrid or electric car near a pedestrian with a white cane. Why should you be extra careful?
choices: Quiet cars are exempt from yielding to pedestrians
Blind pedestrians rely on sound to know a vehicle is near, and a quiet car may not be heard
The pedestrian will rely on seeing your headlights
Quiet cars cannot stop as quickly
explanation: People who are blind listen for traffic. A hybrid or electric vehicle can be very quiet, so take extra care when turning or backing near them.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 48, NY p. 67, MT p. 49)

prompt: An ambulance with flashing lights and a siren is coming up behind you on a two-lane road. What should you do?
choices: Speed up to stay ahead of it
Stop right where you are in your lane
Pull over to the right edge of the road and stop
Pull to the left so it can pass on your right
explanation: Yield to emergency vehicles using a siren and flashing lights: drive to the right edge of the road and stop until they pass.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 51, NY p. 35, MT p. 50)

prompt: Which vehicles must you yield to when they are using a siren and flashing emergency lights?
choices: Only ambulances
Only police cars
Police cars, fire engines, ambulances and other emergency vehicles
Only fire engines
explanation: All authorized emergency vehicles responding with emergency signals get the right-of-way, whether police, fire or ambulance.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 51, NY p. 35, MT p. 50)

prompt: You are in the middle of an intersection when a fire truck with its siren on approaches. What should you do?
choices: Stop right away in the intersection
Back up out of the intersection
Turn left in front of the fire truck to clear the way
Continue through the intersection, then pull to the right and stop
explanation: Do not stop in an intersection for an emergency vehicle. Drive through it, then pull over to the right and stop.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 51, NY p. 35, MT p. 50)

prompt: You have pulled over and stopped for an emergency vehicle. When may you move again?
choices: After it has passed and you have checked that it is safe, watching for other emergency vehicles
As soon as it is beside you
As soon as the siren is off for a moment
Immediately, if you are going in the opposite direction
explanation: Stay stopped until the emergency vehicle has passed. More than one may be responding, so check before you signal and re-enter traffic.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 51, NY p. 35, MT p. 50)

prompt: Traffic is heavy and you cannot pull all the way to the right edge when a police car with siren and lights approaches. What should you do?
choices: Stay in your lane and keep going
Speed up to find a better place to pull over
Move as far to the right as you safely can and stop, leaving it a clear path
Move to the left lane
explanation: The goal is to clear a path. Get as close to the right as is safe and stop until the emergency vehicle passes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 51, NY p. 35, MT p. 50)

prompt: A police car is driving behind you with no siren and no flashing lights on. Must you pull over and stop?
choices: No. The special yield rule applies when an emergency vehicle is using its emergency signals
Yes. You must always pull over for any police car
Yes, but only on a highway
No. Police cars never get the right-of-way
explanation: Emergency vehicles get the right-of-way when they are responding with emergency signals such as a siren or flashing lights. Otherwise, normal traffic rules apply.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 51, NY p. 35, MT p. 50)

prompt: You are already inside a roundabout when an ambulance with its siren on approaches. What should you do?
choices: Stop right where you are inside the roundabout
Back up to the entrance you used
Continue to your exit, leave the roundabout, then pull over
Stop at the next entry point to let it in
explanation: Do not stop inside a roundabout. Drive to your exit, leave the roundabout, then pull to the right and stop to let the emergency vehicle pass.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 46, AL p. 59, NH p. 33)

prompt: A traffic signal is completely dark because of a power outage. How should you treat the intersection?
choices: As if the light were green
As an intersection where main-road traffic never stops
As a yield sign
As an all-way stop
explanation: When a traffic signal is not working, treat the intersection as a four-way (all-way) stop: stop, then go in turn.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 70, FL p. 59, CO p. 10)

prompt: At an intersection where the traffic signal is out, you and a car on your right stop at the same time. Who goes first?
choices: You, because you are on the left
The car on your right
Whichever driver is on the larger street
Whichever driver honks first
explanation: A dark signal is treated as an all-way stop. When two vehicles stop at the same time, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 70, FL p. 59, CO p. 10)

prompt: The signal at a busy intersection has failed and is dark. You are on the main road, which usually gets a long green light. What should you do?
choices: Stop, then go in turn like everyone else at an all-way stop
Keep going, because the main road keeps the right-of-way
Slow down, but do not stop if no one is in the intersection
Keep going, because only the side streets must stop
explanation: With the signal out, every approach must stop. Being on the larger road does not let you skip the stop.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 70, FL p. 59, CO p. 10)

prompt: When entering a roundabout, whom must you yield to?
choices: Traffic waiting to enter at the other entries
No one, if you are going straight
Traffic already in the roundabout
Only vehicles larger than yours
explanation: Drivers entering a roundabout or traffic circle must yield to vehicles already circulating in it, then enter when there is a safe gap.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 46, AL p. 59, NH p. 33)

prompt: Traffic in a U.S. roundabout flows counterclockwise. As you get ready to enter, which way do you look for traffic you must yield to?
choices: To your right
To your left
Straight across the central island
Behind you
explanation: Because traffic circulates counterclockwise, vehicles already in the roundabout approach from your left. Yield to them before entering.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 46, AL p. 59, NH p. 33)

prompt: As you approach a roundabout, a pedestrian is in the crosswalk at the entry. What should you do?
choices: Enter quickly before the pedestrian reaches your lane
Honk, since pedestrians must yield at roundabouts
Stop and let the pedestrian cross before you enter
Go around the pedestrian on the central island
explanation: Before entering a roundabout, yield to pedestrians and bicyclists in the crosswalk, then look left for a gap in circulating traffic.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 46, AL p. 59, NH p. 33)

prompt: You are about to enter a two-lane roundabout. Which traffic must you yield to?
choices: Only traffic in the outer lane
Only traffic in the inner lane
Traffic in all lanes of the roundabout
Only traffic that is about to exit
explanation: Vehicles in any circulating lane may cross your path, so yield to traffic in all lanes before entering a multi-lane roundabout.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 46, AL p. 59, NH p. 33)

prompt: You are driving in a roundabout and a car is waiting to enter. What should you do?
choices: Stop to let the waiting car enter
Keep moving; you have the right-of-way and should not stop unless needed to avoid a crash
Speed up so the waiting car can enter behind you
Change lanes so the car can enter beside you
explanation: Vehicles already in the roundabout have the right-of-way. Stopping inside can cause a crash; stop only to avoid a collision or a pedestrian.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 46, AL p. 59, NH p. 33)

prompt: You are entering a freeway from an on-ramp. Who has the right-of-way?
choices: Traffic already on the freeway
You do, because you are entering
You do, once you turn on your signal
Whichever vehicle is going faster
explanation: Drivers entering a freeway or highway must yield to traffic already on it and merge only when there is a safe gap.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 14, NJ p. 70, AZ p. 31)

prompt: You want to change lanes, but a car is already in that lane next to you. Who has the right-of-way?
choices: The car already in the lane
You, once your signal is on
You, because you are ahead of it
Whichever car is going slower
explanation: You must yield to vehicles already in the lane you want to enter. Do not change lanes if another driver would have to slow down for you.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 14, NJ p. 70, AZ p. 31)

prompt: Your lane is ending ahead and you must merge into the next lane. Who must yield?
choices: Traffic in the continuing lane must stop to let you in
You, the driver whose lane is ending
Whichever driver is going faster
Whichever car is larger
explanation: When merging, you must yield to traffic in the lane you are entering. Adjust your speed, signal, and merge into a safe gap.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 14, NJ p. 70, AZ p. 31)

prompt: You are driving in the right lane of a highway. A car on the on-ramp is trying to merge. What is a helpful thing to do if it is safe?
choices: Move over a lane or adjust your speed to give the merging car room
Speed up so it has to merge behind everyone
Stop in your lane to let it in
Stay beside it so it cannot merge too early
explanation: The merging driver must yield, but as a courtesy you can change lanes or adjust speed to make room, after checking that it is safe to do so.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 14, NJ p. 70, AZ p. 31)

prompt: You are merging from an on-ramp, and a driver on the highway does not move over or slow down for you. What should you do?
choices: Keep going, because highway drivers must make room for you
Merge anyway; the other driver will brake
Adjust your speed and merge behind or ahead of that car when there is a safe gap
Stop in the travel lane and wait
explanation: Making room for merging traffic is a courtesy, not a duty that takes away your obligation to yield. The merging driver must find a safe gap.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 14, NJ p. 70, AZ p. 31)
